Per-row formatting like this is particularly useful for international datasets where different rows may need different currency symbols, date formats, or number conventions. Rather than splitting the data into separate tables by locale, you can handle everything in a single table with targeted formatting calls.


Arguments Common to Several Formatting Methods/Functions
While we can use the fmt_*() methods on a table, we can also use the functional versions of these methods on scalar values or lists of values. These variants exist within the vals module. While arguments across these functions and their corresponding method aren’t exactly the same, there are nonetheless many arguments that are shared among them. Here are some of the most commonly used arguments:

decimals=: set a fixed precision of decimal places
sep_mark=, dec_mark=: set digit separators and the decimal symbol (defaults are "," and ".")
scale_by=: we can choose to scale targeted values by a multiplier value
compact=: larger figures (thousands, millions, etc.) can be autoscaled and decorated with the appropriate suffixes (e.g., "10000" becomes "10K")
pattern=: option to use a text pattern for decoration of the formatted values
locale=: providing a locale ID (e.g., "en", "fr", "de-AT", etc.) will result in numeric formatting specific to the chosen locale

Here are a number of examples that use vals.fmt_number().

fmt_number_1 = vals.fmt_number([1.64, 3.26, 3000.63, 236742.37])
fmt_number_2 = vals.fmt_number([1.64, 3.26, 3000.63, 236742.37], compact=True)
fmt_number_3 = vals.fmt_number([1.64, 3.26, 3000.63, 236742.37], decimals=3)
fmt_number_4 = vals.fmt_number([1.64, 3.26, 3000.63, 236742.37], pattern="[{x}]")
fmt_number_5 = vals.fmt_number([1.64, 3.26, 3000.63, 236742.37], locale="es")

print(fmt_number_1, fmt_number_2, fmt_number_3, fmt_number_4, fmt_number_5, sep="\n")

['1.64', '3.26', '3,000.63', '236,742.37']
['1.64', '3.26', '3.00K', '236.74K']
['1.640', '3.260', '3,000.630', '236,742.370']
['[1.64]', '[3.26]', '[3,000.63]', '[236,742.37]']
['1,64', '3,26', '3000,63', '236.742,37']


Both vals.fmt_number() and vals.fmt_integer() (along with their GT method counterparts) can also group digits with the Indian numbering system by using system="ind". Here, the last three digits are separated and then groups of two follow, which corresponds to thousands, lakhs, and crores. With compact=True, large values are then expressed in lakhs (Lac) and crores (Cr).

fmt_number_ind_1 = vals.fmt_number([3000.63, 236742.37, 12345678.9], system="ind")
fmt_number_ind_2 = vals.fmt_number([3000.63, 236742.37, 12345678.9], system="ind", compact=True)

print(fmt_number_ind_1, fmt_number_ind_2, sep="\n")

['3,000.63', '2,36,742.37', '1,23,45,678.90']
['3,000.63', '2.37 Lac', '1.23 Cr']


Scientific notation can be done with vals.fmt_scientific().

fmt_sci_1 = vals.fmt_scientific([0.00064, 7.353, 863454.63])
fmt_sci_2 = vals.fmt_scientific([1.64, 3.26, 3000.63], decimals=3)
fmt_sci_3 = vals.fmt_scientific([1.64, 3.26, 3000.63], exp_style="E")
fmt_sci_4 = vals.fmt_scientific([1.64, 3.26, 3000.63], locale="de")

print(fmt_sci_1, fmt_sci_2, fmt_sci_3, fmt_sci_4, sep="\n")

["6.40 × 10<sup style='font-size: 65%;'>−4</sup>", '7.35', "8.63 × 10<sup style='font-size: 65%;'>5</sup>"]
['1.640', '3.260', "3.001 × 10<sup style='font-size: 65%;'>3</sup>"]
['1.64E00', '3.26E00', '3.00E03']
['1,64', '3,26', "3,00 × 10<sup style='font-size: 65%;'>3</sup>"]


Dates and times are handled with vals.fmt_date() and vals.fmt_time().

fmt_date_1 = vals.fmt_date(
    ["2015-03-15", "2017-08-18", "2020-04-12"], date_style="wday_month_day_year"
)
fmt_date_2 = vals.fmt_date(["2015-03-15", "2017-08-18", "2020-04-12"], date_style="month_day_year")
fmt_time_1 = vals.fmt_time(["23:03", "00:55", "08:23"], time_style="h_m_p")
fmt_time_2 = vals.fmt_time(["23:03", "00:55", "08:23"], time_style="h_p")

print(fmt_date_1, fmt_date_2, fmt_time_1, fmt_time_2, sep="\n")

['Sunday, March 15, 2015', 'Friday, August 18, 2017', 'Sunday, April 12, 2020']
['March 15, 2015', 'August 18, 2017', 'April 12, 2020']
['11:03 PM', '12:55 AM', '8:23 AM']
['11 PM', '12 AM', '8 AM']


The vals functions are especially handy during development, when you want to quickly test how a formatting option looks without building a full table. Sometimes it’s easier and more convenient to experiment with formatting using the formatting functions in the vals module. There are many options to explore with each type of formatting and so visiting the API Reference is certainly worthwhile.


HTML Escaping of Cell Values
When rendering to HTML, Great Tables automatically escapes special characters (<, >, &, ", ') in body cells that have not been processed by a fmt_*() method. This prevents cross-site scripting (XSS) when displaying untrusted data (e.g., user-submitted text, CSV uploads) in web applications, dashboards, or reports.
Cells that have been formatted (e.g., with fmt_number(), fmt_markdown(), fmt_image(), etc.) are treated as trusted HTML and are not escaped. This allows formatters to produce rich HTML content like images, links, and styled text.
To include raw HTML or Markdown in cells that would otherwise be escaped, use a formatting method with the html() or md() helpers:

import polars as pl
from great_tables import html, md

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "plain": ["x & y", "a < b"],
    "rich_html": ["<b>bold</b>", "<em>italic</em>"],
    "rich_md": ["**bold**", "*italic*"],
})

(
    GT(df)
    .fmt(columns="rich_html", fns=lambda x: html(x).to_html())
    .fmt(columns="rich_md", fns=lambda x: md(x).to_html())
)







  plain
  rich_html
  rich_md



  
    x & y
    bold
    bold
  
  
    a < b
    italic
    italic
  







In the table above, the plain column values are automatically escaped (e.g., & becomes &), while the rich_html and rich_md column values are rendered as HTML because they were processed through fmt() with the html() and md() helpers respectively.
For finer control, fmt_passthrough() marks cells as formatted without transforming their values. By default it escapes special characters (just like unformatted cells), but you can set escape=False to pass values through as raw HTML. It also accepts a pattern= argument for decorating values:

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "safe_text": ["x & y", "a < b"],
    "raw_html": ["<b>bold</b>", "<em>italic</em>"],
    "decorated": ["ABC", "DEF"],
})

(
    GT(df)
    .fmt_passthrough(columns="safe_text")
    .fmt_passthrough(columns="raw_html", escape=False)
    .fmt_passthrough(columns="decorated", pattern="[{x}]")
)







  safe_text
  raw_html
  decorated



  
    x & y
    bold
    [ABC]
  
  
    a < b
    italic
    [DEF]
  







The same escaping applies to row group labels, summary row labels, column labels, the title and subtitle, footnotes, and source notes. In all of these places, wrap the text in md() or html() when you do want it interpreted as Markdown or HTML.


Conclusion
Formatting is one of the most impactful things you can do to improve a table’s readability. With the fmt_*() methods on a GT object and the corresponding functions in the vals module, you have a comprehensive toolkit for turning raw values into polished, publication-ready content.

title: Glossary
text:
Terms used throughout the Great Tables documentation, listed alphabetically. Where a term has a direct counterpart in the API, the relevant class, method, or module is noted.



Body

The main data area of the table, consisting of rows and columns of cells that hold the underlying data values (after any formatting or substitution has been applied). The body excludes the header, column header, stub, footer, and any summary rows. Targetable with loc.body().

Cell

A single value at the intersection of a row and a column within the body, stub, or summary rows. Cells are the fundamental unit that formatters, styles, and footnotes act upon.

Column controls

In a GTI table, the small controls under each column label: the column’s dtype (with i_inspect()), its sort arrows (with i_sorting(), on by default), and its filter button (with i_cols_filter()). What readers can do with each column (sort, search, resize, hide, move or group by it) is set with i_cols_controls().

Column header

The region directly above the body that contains all column labels and any spanner labels. It provides the labeling structure that maps data columns to their display names and groupings. Targetable as a whole with loc.column_header().

Column labels

The individual text labels that identify each column in the table. By default they are the column names from the input DataFrame, but they can be overridden with cols_label() or transformed with cols_label_with(). Targetable with loc.column_labels().

Column profile

In a GTI table, a small plot under a column label showing how the column’s values are spread: a histogram for numbers and dates, and bars for the most common values of other columns, with the share of missing values. Profiles follow the rows the search and filters keep. Added with i_cols_profile().

Column selector

An expression passed to a columns= parameter to identify which columns an operation should act on. Accepts a column name (string), a list of names, an integer index, a Polars selector expression (e.g., cs.numeric()), or a callable that takes a column name and returns a boolean. Column selectors are used throughout the API in methods like fmt_number(), cols_align(), tab_style(), and many others.

Control bar

The row of controls just below a GTI table that brings together what readers can do with the table as a whole: the search and keyboard shortcuts, the page controls, the query button ({ }), the buttons that open the table’s panels, undo and redo (see view state), and a Reset button once the view has changed. A table made with opt_interactive() has a pager instead.

Data color

A technique for colorizing cell backgrounds based on data values, providing a visual encoding of magnitude or category directly in the table. Applied with data_color(), which supports custom palettes, ColorBrewer palettes, domain specification, and automatic contrasting text color.

Filter

In an interactive table, a control that keeps only the rows matching a condition on one column, opened from the column’s filter button. A GTI table gets filters with i_cols_filter(), of five types: "text", "facet" (a checklist of values), "range", "date", and "bool". A row is shown when it passes every filter and the search.

Filter tokens

In a GTI table, a token for each filter in use, shown below the table, that says which rows the filter keeps. A token’s ✕ removes its filter.

Footer

The bottom region of the table, below the body and any summary rows. It contains footnotes and source notes. Targetable as a whole with loc.footer().

Footnote

An annotation consisting of two linked parts: a footnote mark placed at a specific location in the table, and the corresponding footnote text rendered in the footer. Added with tab_footnote(). When multiple footnotes share the same text, the mark is reused rather than duplicated.

Footnote mark

A small symbol (number, letter, or typographic symbol) attached to a cell or label in the table that links it to its corresponding footnote text in the footer. Marks are ordered left-to-right, top-to-bottom according to their position in the table. The mark style is configured with opt_footnote_marks(), which accepts keywords like "numbers" (the default), "letters", "LETTERS", "standard" (four traditional symbols), or "extended" (six symbols), as well as custom lists of strings.

Formatter

A method that transforms how raw data values are displayed in cells without altering the underlying data. All built-in formatters follow the fmt_*() naming convention (e.g., fmt_number(), fmt_currency(), fmt_date()). A general-purpose fmt() method accepts a custom formatting function. The vals module provides standalone equivalents for use outside a GT object, such as in summary rows definitions.

Grand summary rows

Aggregation rows that summarize the entire table’s data, regardless of row groups. Created with grand_summary_rows() and placed at the very bottom of the body (above the footer). Targetable with loc.grand_summary().

GT object

The central object in Great Tables, created by passing a Polars, Pandas, or PyArrow table to GT(). All table-building operations are methods on this object and return a modified copy, enabling method chaining. Optional constructor arguments include rowname_col (to create a stub), groupname_col (to create row groups), locale, and id.

GTI table

An interactive table made with GTI() rather than GT(), built like a GT object and rendered as a table readers work with. Its i_ methods set what readers can do with it, column by column: which filters they get, which columns they can hide, move or pin, how they can export the rows, and how the table is first shown (its view). GTI.from_gt() turns a GT table into a GTI table.

Header

The topmost region of the table, positioned above the column header. It contains the title and optionally a subtitle. Set with tab_header(). Targetable as a whole with loc.header().

Height handle

In a GTI table whose body scrolls within a set height (with i_scroll()), the handle at the foot of the body that readers drag for a taller or shorter body. A double click on it restores the set height.

Hidden column

A column that is present in the underlying data but not rendered in the output table. Columns can be hidden with cols_hide() and restored with cols_unhide(). Hidden columns remain accessible for operations like merged columns patterns, data color mapping, and from_column() references.

Interactive table

A table that readers can sort, search, filter, and page through in the browser, with no server or other library needed. It’s made either by adding opt_interactive() to a GT table’s method chain, for a published table that readers can browse, or as a GTI table, for a table that is an interface. Both keep the table’s formatting, styles, and structure.

Linked tables

GTI tables on the same page that work together through i_link(): the rows a reader selects in one (see selection) filter the others to the rows with the same values in a shared column.

Locale

A language/region identifier (e.g., "en", "de", "fr-CA") that controls how formatters render numbers, currencies, dates, and times. Locale determines things like the decimal mark, digit grouping separator, currency symbol, and date/time patterns. Set at the table level with GT(locale=...) or with_locale(), or overridden per formatter call.

Location selector

An object from the loc module that identifies a specific region or set of cells in the table. Location selectors are used in tab_style() to target where styles are applied and in tab_footnote() to place footnote marks. Examples include loc.body(), loc.column_labels(), loc.stub(), and loc.header().

Merged columns

A display technique that combines content from multiple columns into a single column using a pattern string. Created with cols_merge(), where the pattern uses {0}, {1}, etc. to reference column values (e.g., "{0} ({1})"). Conditional removal of content when values are missing is supported via <</>> delimiters in the pattern. Convenience variants include cols_merge_uncert(), cols_merge_range(), and cols_merge_n_pct().

Nanoplot

A tiny inline visualization embedded directly in a table cell via fmt_nanoplot(). Supports "line", "bar", and "boxplot" plot types, with optional reference lines, reference areas, and automatic y-axis scaling across rows. Appearance is customized through nanoplot_options().

Page controls

In a GTI table’s control bar, the buttons for the first, previous, next, and last pages, around the page counter (“1 / 2”), which can be clicked to type the page to go to. The page size is set with i_pagination().

Pager

The page buttons and row count below a table made with opt_interactive(), in place of a GTI table’s control bar. Its style is set with opt_interactive(pagination_type=...).

Panel

In a GTI table, a box opened from a button in the control bar: the Columns panel (to hide and move columns), the grouping panel (to group the rows by a column), the export panel (from i_export()), and the info panel, which says how the table is sorted and can go back to the view it was first shown with.

Pinned columns

In a wide GTI table that scrolls sideways, columns that stay in view, on the left (after the stub, which always stays) or on the right. Set with i_cols_pin().

Preheader

Optional content rendered above the table element itself (before the header). Set via tab_header(preheader=...). Accepts raw HTML strings and is useful for adding non-tabular content like badges or links that sit outside the table’s visual boundaries.

Preset

The settings a GTI table starts with, chosen with GTI(preset=...): "report" (the default), for a table to be read, or "explorer", for looking through data, with every column filtered, profiled, hideable and movable, compact monospaced rows, CSV export, and the row numbers and status line of i_inspect(). The i_ methods change a preset as they would any table.

Query

A GTI table’s filters written as text, such as mfr in ("Ferrari") and hp >= 600. The { } button in the control bar opens the query for readers to edit, and ~~GTI.i_view(filter=...) takes one to set the filters the table starts with.

Responsive layout

How a GTI table fits a container narrower than itself, set with i_responsive(): "scroll" (the table scrolls sideways), "stack" (each row becomes a card, below stack_below= pixels), or "collapse" (columns are dropped by their priority from i_cols_priority(), and each row gets a button showing what was dropped). The default, "auto", picks one from the table’s columns.

Row details

In a GTI table, more content for each row, shown under it when the reader clicks the arrow by the row (or uses Expand all in the info panel). Made from each row’s values by a function given to i_row_details(), or taken from a column.

Row group

A categorical label that divides the body into logical sections of rows. Row groups appear as spanning labels across the full width of the table. Created by passing groupname_col= to GT() and ordered with row_group_order(). Targetable with loc.row_groups().

Row numbers

In a GTI table with i_inspect(), the number at the start of each row giving its place in the data, which stays with the row as the table is sorted and filtered. A DataFrame’s rows are numbered from 0 and a database’s from 1, unless row_start= says otherwise.

Row selector

An expression passed to a rows= parameter to identify which rows an operation should act on. Accepts an integer index, a list of indices, a list of row names (when a stub is present), a Polars expression, or a callable. Row selectors are used in methods like fmt_number(), tab_style(), cols_merge(), and others.

Search

In an interactive table, a field that keeps the rows with what’s typed in any searchable column’s cells, as the table shows them, ignoring case and accents. In a GTI table it’s in the control bar (with i_search(), on by default) and is opened with /.

Selection

The rows a reader has selected in a GTI table with i_selection(), by clicking the rows or their checkboxes (one row with "single", any number with "multiple"). The selection links linked tables, can be exported, and can be read from Python.

Source note

Citation or attribution text displayed in the footer, below any footnotes. Added with tab_source_note() and supports md() and html() formatting. Multiple source notes can be added and appear in the order they were defined. Targetable with loc.source_notes().

Spanner label

A label in the column header that spans across multiple contiguous column labels, providing a higher-level grouping. Created with tab_spanner() or automatically with tab_spanner_delim() (which splits column names at a delimiter character), and relabeled with tab_spanner_label_with(). Spanners can be nested to any depth. Targetable with loc.spanner_labels().

Status line

In a GTI table with i_inspect(), the line just above the table saying what the data is and how much of it is shown (e.g., “Polars DataFrame · 12 of 47 rows × 4 columns”).

Stub

A reserved leftmost column of the table that holds row labels, visually set apart from the body by a vertical dividing line. Created by passing rowname_col= to GT(). The stub provides a way to name rows and is required for row-based selection by name. Targetable with loc.stub(). The stub sentinel object (importable from great_tables) can be used in cols_width() to set the stub column’s width.

Stubhead

The cell at the top-left corner of the table, at the intersection of the stub and the column header. It exists only when a stub is present and can be labeled with tab_stubhead(). Targetable with loc.stubhead().

Style

A visual property applied to table elements via tab_style(). Styles are defined using objects from the style module: style.text() for text properties (color, font, size, weight, alignment), style.fill() for background color, style.borders() for cell borders, and style.css() for arbitrary CSS. Styles are paired with location selectors to target specific parts of the table.

Subtitle

Secondary descriptive text displayed below the title in the header. Set via tab_header(subtitle=...). Supports md() and html() formatting. Targetable with loc.subtitle().

Summary rows

Aggregation rows placed within each row group that summarize that group’s data. Created with summary_rows(), which accepts aggregation functions (Polars expressions or callables) and an optional formatter. Can be placed at the top or bottom of each group with the side= parameter. Targetable with loc.summary().

Table theme

A coordinated set of visual options that control the overall appearance of the table. Great Tables provides 36 premade themes via opt_stylize(), combining 6 visual styles with 6 color palettes. Fine-grained control over every aspect of the table’s appearance is available through tab_options().

Title

The main heading text displayed at the top of the header. Set via tab_header(title=...). Supports md() and html() formatting. Targetable with loc.title().

View

How a reader has a GTI table set up: its filters, sort, search, page, page size, hidden columns, the column its rows are grouped by, and the height of a body that scrolls. The view the table starts with is set with i_view(). See also view state.

View state

A GTI table’s view as it’s kept with i_view_state(): in the page’s URL, so a reloaded or shared page opens the table as it was, and optionally in the browser’s storage (storage=True). It also gives the control bar undo and redo buttons. Keeping the view in the URL needs a table ID.

title: GTI in Python and Apps
text:
An interactive table works in the browser on its own, but Python can also read what readers do with it, and change it: in a notebook, with a GTI table (see GTI Tables) as a widget; in a marimo notebook or app, as a UI element; and in Shiny, Streamlit, Panel and Solara apps. These take a GTI table or a GT table with opt_interactive(), get its view and selection, and can set them. A page an app makes itself (with Flask, Django or FastHTML) shows the table as it works in the browser, with its runtime included once, however many tables the page has. The notebook, marimo, Streamlit and Panel examples can each be run here, in the browser, without installing anything; the Solara and Flask apps, which need a server, are shown as they look when they’re run.




Using the table from Python
In a notebook, i_as_widget() shows the table as a widget (with anywidget, installed with pip install great_tables[widget]), whose view and selection Python can read and set: what the reader searched for, filtered and sorted by, the rows that leaves, and the rows they selected. The table still works in the browser; the widget tells Python what it shows.
from great_tables import GT, GTI, data

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
widget = (
    GTI(cars)
    .fmt_integer("hp")
    .fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_responsive("scroll")
    .i_as_widget()
)
widget
With i_responsive() set to "scroll", the table scrolls sideways in a narrow container (as on a phone), rather than its rows being stacked as cards (see Narrow containers), as each app’s table on this page does.
Then, in another cell (as the browser gives Python the table’s state once the cell is done), the cars selected, as a table of their own:
chosen = widget.view(selected=True)
print(f"{len(chosen)} of {len(widget.rows)} cars selected")
GT(chosen).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
widget.query is the filters, as a query in text (e.g., 'mfr in ("Ferrari")'), widget.search the search and widget.sort the sort (e.g., ["-hp"]). widget.rows is the data rows kept, in the order shown (numbered from 0), and widget.view() gives those rows as a DataFrame of the data’s library (and widget.view(selected=True) the rows selected). Setting query, search, sort or selection changes the table as shown:
widget.query = 'mfr in ("Ferrari", "Lamborghini")'
widget.sort = "-hp"
widget.selection = []
widget.on_change(callback) calls callback(widget) after each change the reader makes. A change made from Python is applied by the browser after the cell runs, so ask for the rows it leaves in another cell.
Here’s that notebook, run in the browser (in JupyterLite, with these docs’ Great Tables). Run its cells in turn, select a few cars, and then run the cells below the table. It’s also in Great Tables’ repository, as demos/widget/cars.ipynb, which can be opened in Colab.



Using the table in a marimo notebook or app
In a marimo notebook (or one run as an app), mo_gti(), from great_tables.marimo (installed with pip install great_tables[marimo]), shows an interactive table (a GTI table, or a GT table with opt_interactive()) as a UI element, like marimo’s own. Assigned to a variable, the cells that read it run again with each change the reader makes. Its value is a dict of the table’s "query", "search" and "sort", the data "rows" kept (in the order shown) and the rows in its "selection". Setting the element’s query, search, sort or selection (as in a button’s on_click=) changes the table, and the cells that read it then run again.
import marimo as mo

from great_tables import GT, GTI, data
from great_tables.marimo import mo_gti

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
table = mo_gti(
    GTI(cars)
    .fmt_integer("hp")
    .fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_responsive("scroll")
)
table
Then, in other cells, a button that sorts the table by horsepower, and the cars selected, as a table of their own:
def fastest(_):
    table.sort = "-hp"
    table.selection = []

fastest_button = mo.ui.button(label="Fastest first", on_click=fastest)
fastest_button
chosen = table.view(selected=True)
mo.vstack(
    [
        mo.md(f"{len(chosen)} of {len(table.value['rows'] or [])} cars selected"),
        GT(chosen).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0),
    ]
)
Here’s that notebook, run as an app in the browser (with marimo’s WebAssembly export, and these docs’ Great Tables). Select a few cars, filter by manufacturer, or click “Fastest first”:

table.view() gives the rows kept as a DataFrame of the data’s library (and table.view(selected=True) the rows selected). The rows are found by the browser, as the table works there. Before the table is shown, Python finds them, except for a GT table with opt_interactive() or a table that starts with a search: their rows are None until the browser has shown the table. They’re also None after the table’s view is set (as by the button), until the browser has applied it. Running the table’s cell again makes a new table, which starts as it’s made. A table whose rows are kept in Python (with i_scale()) asks the notebook for each page instead, and its rows are always found in Python.


Using the table in a Shiny app
In a Shiny app, an interactive table (a GTI table, or a GT table with opt_interactive()) rendered with render_gt(), from great_tables.shiny, gives the server its state as inputs, named after the output: input.<id>_view() (a dict with the "query", "search", "sort", "page", "page_size", "hidden" columns and "group_by" column), input.<id>_rows() (the data rows kept, in the order shown) and input.<id>_selection() (the rows selected). update_gti() sets its query, search, sort and selection from the server.
from shiny import App, reactive, render, ui
from great_tables import GTI, data
from great_tables.shiny import output_gt, render_gt, update_gti

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_action_button("fastest", "Fastest first"),
    output_gt("cars"),
    ui.output_text("chosen"),
)


def server(input, output, session):
    @render_gt
    def cars():
        return (
            GTI(data.pl.gtcars.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]))
            .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
            .i_selection("multiple")
            .i_responsive("scroll")
        )

    @render.text
    def chosen():
        rows = input.cars_selection()
        return f"{len(rows)} of {len(input.cars_rows())} cars selected"

    @reactive.effect
    @reactive.event(input.fastest)
    def _():
        update_gti("cars", sort="-hp", selection=[])


app = App(app_ui, server)
The table works in the browser as it does anywhere else, so the server isn’t asked for each page, sort or search; a table rendered again starts with the view it’s given.


Using the table in a Streamlit app
In a Streamlit app, st_gti(), from great_tables.streamlit (installed with pip install great_tables[streamlit]), shows an interactive table (a GTI table, or a GT table with opt_interactive()) and gives its state: its query, search and sort, the data rows kept (in the order shown) and the rows in its selection. Each change the reader makes runs the app again, with the table’s new state. update_gti(), called in a widget’s callback, sets its query, search, sort and selection from the app. Here, the cars selected are charted, and shown as a table of their own (a GT table’s HTML, with st.html()):
import streamlit as st

from great_tables import GT, GTI, data
from great_tables.streamlit import st_gti, update_gti

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]

st.button("Fastest first", on_click=update_gti, args=("cars",), kwargs={"sort": "-hp"})
table = (
    GTI(cars)
    .fmt_integer("hp")
    .fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_responsive("scroll")
)
state = st_gti(table, key="cars")
st.write(f"{len(state.selection)} of {len(state.rows or [])} cars selected")

chosen = cars.iloc[state.selection]
st.bar_chart(chosen, x="model", y="hp")
st.html(GT(chosen).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0).as_raw_html())
Here’s that app, run in the browser (with stlite, and these docs’ Great Tables):

The table keeps its view and selection by its key as the app runs again, as long as it’s rendered the same. A table whose rows are kept in Python (with i_scale()) asks the app for each page, which runs it again; make it once, with st.cache_resource, so that it isn’t rendered again each time.


Using the table in a Panel app
In a Panel app or notebook, GTIPane, from great_tables.panel (installed with pip install great_tables[panel]), shows an interactive table (a GTI table, or a GT table with opt_interactive()) as a Panel component, whose state is in its parameters: query, search and sort (a list, e.g., ["-hp"], which can be set to a column name, "-hp", too), the data rows kept (in the order shown) and the rows in its selection. Each change the reader makes sets them, so that they can be used with pn.bind() or watched like any other parameter; and setting query, search, sort or selection changes the table. Here, the cars selected are shown as a table of their own, bound to the table’s rows and selection:
import panel as pn

from great_tables import GT, GTI, data
from great_tables.panel import GTIPane

pn.extension()

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
table = GTIPane(
    GTI(cars)
    .fmt_integer("hp")
    .fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_responsive("scroll")
)


def chosen(rows, selection):
    picked = GT(cars.iloc[selection]).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    return pn.Column(f"{len(selection)} of {len(rows or [])} cars selected", pn.pane.HTML(picked))


fastest = pn.widgets.Button(name="Fastest first")
fastest.on_click(lambda _: table.param.update(sort=["-hp"], selection=[]))
pn.Column(fastest, table, pn.bind(chosen, table.param.rows, table.param.selection)).servable()
Here’s that app, run in the browser (converted with panel convert, with these docs’ Great Tables):

table.data() gives the rows kept as a DataFrame of the data’s library (and table.data(selected=True) the rows selected). The rows are found by the browser, as the table works there. Before the table is shown, Python finds them, except for a GT table with opt_interactive() or a table that starts with a search: their rows are None until the browser has shown the table. A table whose rows are kept in Python (with i_scale()) asks the app for each page instead, and its rows are always found in Python.


Using the table in a Solara app
In a Solara app or notebook, the GTITable component, from great_tables.solara (installed with pip install great_tables[solara]), shows an interactive table (a GTI table, or a GT table with opt_interactive()), whose query, search, sort (a list, e.g., ["-hp"]) and selection are the app’s values, as with Solara’s own components. Each can be a reactive variable, which each change the reader makes sets and which changes the table when the app sets it, or a value with a callback (on_query=, on_sort=, …). One that isn’t given starts as the table has it. The data rows kept (in the order shown) are given to on_rows=. Here, the cars selected are shown as a table of their own (a GT table’s HTML, with solara.HTML()):
import solara

from great_tables import GT, GTI, data
from great_tables.solara import GTITable

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
table = (
    GTI(cars)
    .fmt_integer("hp")
    .fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_responsive("scroll")
)

sort = solara.reactive([])
selection = solara.reactive([])
rows = solara.reactive([])


def fastest():
    sort.set(["-hp"])
    selection.set([])


@solara.component
def Page():
    solara.Button("Fastest first", on_click=fastest)
    GTITable(table, sort=sort, selection=selection, on_rows=rows.set)
    solara.Text(f"{len(selection.value)} of {len(rows.value)} cars selected")

    chosen = GT(cars.iloc[selection.value]).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    solara.HTML(unsafe_innerHTML=chosen.as_raw_html())
Saved as app.py, it’s run with solara run app.py (with Great Tables, Solara and Pandas installed), or with uv, which installs them for the app:
uv run --with "great_tables[solara]" --with pandas \
  solara run app.py
It’s also in Great Tables’ repository, as demos/solara/app.py. Run, with two cars selected, it looks like this:



The Solara app, with two cars selected


The component keeps the table’s view as the app renders again, as long as it’s given the same table or one rendered the same. A table whose rows are kept in Python (with i_scale()) asks the app for each page, and its rows are found in Python; make it once (at the module’s top level, as here, or with solara.use_memo()), so that it isn’t rendered again each time.


Using the table in a page an app makes
An app that makes its own pages, with templates (as Flask and Django apps do) or with FastHTML, shows an interactive table as its HTML, which as_raw_html() gives: the table’s <gt-table> element, followed by the runtime that makes it interactive (its JavaScript and CSS). The table works in the browser, as in an HTML file, without asking the app for anything. A table put in a Jinja template (as Flask’s are, { table }) or in a FastHTML component (Div(table)), or returned by a FastHTML route on its own, is shown as its HTML, as it is.
A page with several tables needs the runtime only once: runtime_tags(), from great_tables.web, gives it, for the page’s <head>, and each table is then given without it, with as_raw_html(runtime="none"). With url=, the tags link to the runtime’s files, which write_runtime() writes for the app to serve, so that a browser keeps them as it does any other file. Here, they’re written to the folder Flask serves as /static/ (app.static_folder, beside the app, wherever it’s run from):
from flask import Flask, render_template_string
from markupsafe import Markup

from great_tables import GTI, data
from great_tables.web import runtime_tags, write_runtime

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
app = Flask(__name__)
write_runtime(f"{app.static_folder}/gti")

PAGE = """
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>{{ runtime }}</head>
<body>{% for table in tables %}{{ table }}{% endfor %}</body>
</html>
"""


@app.route("/")
def index():
    table = GTI(cars).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0).i_responsive("scroll")
    tables = [table.i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet"), table.i_selection("multiple")]
    return render_template_string(
        PAGE,
        runtime=runtime_tags(url="/static/gti/"),
        tables=[Markup(table.as_raw_html(runtime="none")) for table in tables],
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()
Saved as app.py, it’s run with python app.py (or flask --app app.py run, with Great Tables, Flask and Pandas installed), or with uv:
uv run --with great_tables --with flask --with pandas app.py
It’s also in Great Tables’ repository, as demos/flask/app.py. Its page, with two cars selected in the second table, looks like this:



The Flask app’s page, with two cars selected in its second table


Django makes what’s put in a template a string before it’s shown, so a table is given as its HTML, marked safe (with mark_safe(table.as_raw_html()), or { table_html|safe } in the template); the runtime’s tags are shown as they are. In FastHTML, the HTML of a table without its runtime is given as NotStr(table.as_raw_html(runtime="none")), and the tags as one of the app’s headers (fast_app(hdrs=(runtime_tags(),))).
A page whose Content Security Policy allows no inline scripts can have the runtime from its files (script-src 'self'), or inline with the policy’s nonce (runtime_tags(nonce=...)); the table’s spec, in a <script type="application/json">, is data, which isn’t run. The table’s own CSS is inline, so the policy’s style-src must allow 'unsafe-inline'. A table whose rows are kept in Python (with i_scale()) needs an app that answers its asks for pages, so in a page an app makes, its rows are in the browser.

title: GTI Tables
text:
When readers need more than opt_interactive() gives them (see Making Tables Interactive), make the table a GTI table. Here, the Make column gets a list of its values to choose from and HP a range, the table is first shown with the most powerful cars at the top, and readers can download the rows they’ve filtered as CSV.

import polars as pl
from great_tables import GTI, data

gtcars_pl = data.pl.gtcars.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "trq", "msrp"])

(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: as a GTI table")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="hp")
    .i_view(sort="-hp")
    .i_export("csv")
)

Each of the i_ methods has examples on its reference page (e.g., i_cols_filter()), and the API Reference has them all.

The parts of a GTI table
A GTI table is the table GT made, with a few parts added around it. Here they are in teal, on a table that’s filtered by mfr, sorted by hp and scrolls within a set height:



From the top:

The status line, just above the table, says what the data is and how much of it is shown (“Polars DataFrame · 12 of 47 rows × 4 columns”). It’s there with i_inspect() (and in an explorer). In a table made with opt_interactive(use_search=True), the search box is here too.
The column controls, under each column label: the column’s dtype (with i_inspect()), its sort arrows (with i_sorting(), on by default), and its filter button (with i_cols_filter()).
The column profiles, under the labels of the columns i_cols_profile() chose: a small plot of how their values are spread.
The row numbers, at the start of each row (with i_inspect()), which stay with the rows as they’re sorted and filtered. A DataFrame’s rows are numbered from 0, as its index is, and a DuckDB relation’s or an Ibis table’s from 1, as a database numbers them; row_start= in i_inspect() sets either one.
The height handle, at the foot of a body that scrolls (with i_scroll()), dragged for a taller or shorter body.
The filter tokens, one for each filter the rows are filtered by, which say what it keeps; a token’s ✕ removes its filter.
The control bar, just below the table, which brings together what readers can do with the table as a whole. From its left, it has:

the search (with i_search(), on by default) and the table’s keyboard shortcuts
the page controls, around the page counter (“1 / 2”), which can be clicked to type a page to go to
the filters as text button ({ }, in a table with filters), which opens the filters as a query to edit, in the form i_view() takes them (with filter=)
the buttons that open the table’s panels: its columns, grouping its rows and exporting them (when the table has these), and its info
undo and redo (with i_view_state()), and a Reset button once the view has changed


A table made with opt_interactive() has a pager below it instead of the control bar: its page buttons, and the number of rows shown.
The status line and the control bar are close to the table, and the space that GT (or the page) leaves around the table is kept past them, so that they read as part of it rather than of the text around it.
A table names its own parts too: press ? with the table focused (click in it first), or use Name the table’s parts in its info panel, and each part it has is outlined, with its name beside it. ? again, Escape, or a click outside the table puts the names away.
For a page that shows readers the parts, as this one does, i_display() with parts=True names them from the start, and for good. Here’s the table above, live: it works as ever under the names, which follow its parts as you sort, filter, page or scroll it.

(
    GTI(gtcars_pl, id="gtcars-parts")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_inspect()
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_profile(columns="hp")
    .i_view(filter='mfr in ("Ferrari", "Lamborghini")', sort="-hp")
    .i_view_state()
    .i_scroll(260)
    .i_display(parts=True)
)

Filtering the rows
Each column given to i_cols_filter() gets a filter button under its label, which opens its filter. The filter’s type goes by the column’s values, unless type= names one:

"text" keeps the rows whose cell has what’s typed, as the table shows it, ignoring case and accents (as the search does)
"facet" is a checklist of the column’s values, each with its number of rows (of those the other filters and the search keep); it’s what a categorical column gets, and a text column with only a few values, each repeated
"range" keeps the numbers from one to another (at least one, at most the other), for a column of numbers
"date" keeps the dates from one to another, picked in date fields (or date and time fields, for a column of dates and times)
"bool" keeps the rows that are true, false or missing, each with its number of rows, for a column of booleans

Facets, ranges, dates and booleans go by the column’s values, not by how they’re formatted. Here are the half-hourly readings of May 2023 at Gibraltar’s airport, with a column of dates and times made from the dataset’s text, and one saying whether there were gusts. The conditions get a text filter (there are 22 of them, too many for a list), the times a date filter, the numbers ranges and the gusts a bool filter. The table starts with the rainy readings from the 20th on; open the Time filter to change the dates, or the Gusts filter for only the readings with gusts.

weather = (

A row is shown when it passes every filter, and the search. The tokens below the table show the filters that are on, and the { } button in the control bar opens them as text, a query to edit (with suggestions as you type), as i_view() takes it with filter=. Its clauses are a column name and then:

contains and a string, for a text filter (condition contains "rain"), or matches and a regular expression between slashes (condition matches /^light/i)
in and values in parentheses, for a facet or a bool filter (gusts in (true))
>=, <=, > or < and a number, for a range (temp >= 25), or a date in double quotes, for a date filter (when < "2023-05-08"); or top or bottom and a whole number, for the rows with the largest or smallest values (wind_speed top 10)
is null, for the rows missing a value, whatever the filter

The clauses are joined by and, and groups are written with or, not and parentheses (temp >= 25 or (gusts in (true) and not condition contains "fair")); not in, not contains and is not null can be written as such. A column name that isn’t letters, digits and underscores goes in backticks. A query in i_view() is checked against the columns’ filters when the table is shown, so a clause on a column without a filter, or with a filter of another type, is an error.
While the query is open, each filtered column’s name is shown under its label, and a click on one puts it in at the caret. Tab (or ↓) lists the columns where one can go. A column’s label can be typed in place of its name (unless another column has the same label): as its words joined by underscores, or as it is in backticks, so a column labeled Country of origin can be typed as country_of_origin. The name is put in its place as the word ends. The URL and i_view() take only names.


Sorting by several columns, and the keyboard
A click on a column’s sort arrows (or its label) sorts the table by it: once for ascending order, again for descending, and a third time for the table’s own order. With Shift held, a click adds the column to the sort, so that it sorts the rows the columns before it leave tied, and the arrows are numbered in the order the columns sort the rows. Here, the cars are sorted by their make and then from the most powerful down; Shift-click Year to sort the cars that tie by year as well, or click HP alone to sort by it only. The info panel (from the (i) button) says how the table is sorted, and can put it back in its own order.

(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: sorted by make, then horsepower")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_view(sort=["mfr", "-hp"])
)

i_view() takes the sort as a list of columns, the first sorting the rows and the next the rows that tie, each with a - before it for descending order. Missing values are last either way.
The table’s controls are buttons and fields, reached with Tab, and with the table clicked (or focus in it) these keys work too:

/ opens the search, and Esc clears it, then closes it
← and → go to the previous or next page, and Home and End to the first or last
Shift and a click sorts by more than one column, and (with i_selection()) selects a range of rows
Alt (⌥ on a Mac) with ↑ or ↓ moves a column, in the Columns panel
Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y (⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z on a Mac) undo and redo a change to the view, with i_view_state()
? names the table’s parts

The keyboard button at the start of the control bar lists the keys the table has.


Selecting rows
With i_selection(), readers can select rows, by clicking them or their checkboxes, in a column before the others. With "multiple" (the method’s default), Shift and a click selects the rows from the last one clicked, and the checkbox in the column labels selects every row the search and filters keep (on every page, not only the one shown); with "single", selecting a row clears the one selected before. The info panel says how many rows are selected, and its Clear button clears them. Here, select a few cars, then open the export panel: with Selected rows only checked, only they’re exported.

The selection stays as the rows are sorted, searched, filtered and paged. It’s what links tables together (see Linked tables), and Python can read it, with the table as a widget or in an app (see GTI in Python and Apps).


Keeping the view
With i_view_state(), the reader’s view of the table (its filters, sort, search, page, page size, hidden columns, the column its rows are grouped by, and the height of a body that scrolls) is kept as they change it: in the page’s URL, by default, so that reloading the page, or sharing its link, opens the table as it was; and with storage=True, in the browser’s storage too, so that the reader finds the table as they left it when they come back to the page. The view is kept by the table’s ID, so the table needs one (from GTI(id=), or with_id()). Here, choose a make or two and sort the cars, then look at the page’s address, and reload the page.

In the URL, each part of the view is in the query string, named after the table’s ID (as in ?gtcars-kept.filter=mfr+in+(%22Ferrari%22)&gtcars-kept.sort=-hp, the filter written as text), so tables with different IDs keep their own views, and the page’s other parameters are left alone. A link with a table’s view opens it with that view, rather than the one in the browser’s storage. A part of a view the table can’t have (say, a filter on a column that no longer has one) is left out, with a warning in the browser’s console. The rows selected and the columns’ widths aren’t kept.
The control bar has undo and redo buttons (and Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y, or ⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z on a Mac), and the info panel a button that goes back to the view the table is first shown with. Undo alone, i_view_state(url=False), doesn’t need an ID.


Scrolling in place
With i_scroll(), the table takes up no more than a set height, and its body scrolls within it. The table’s header and column labels stay in view, each group’s heading sticks below them while its rows go by, and the grand summary rows at the bottom stick to the bottom. Footnotes and source notes scroll with the body. Here are all 47 cars, with pagination off, in a body 400 pixels high.

from great_tables import vals

gtcars_grouped = data.pl.gtcars.select(["ctry_origin", "mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "trq"])

(
    GTI(gtcars_grouped, rowname_col="model", groupname_col="ctry_origin")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: scrolling in place")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .grand_summary_rows(fns={"Average": pl.col("hp", "trq").mean()}, fmt=vals.fmt_integer)
    .i_pagination(False)
    .i_scroll(400)
)

On one line, a column of text is as wide as most of its cells need, rather than as wide as its longest: the longest tenth of them are cut short, and a cut cell shows its text in a tooltip as the pointer rests on it (or as it’s tapped). Numbers left unformatted are kept short in any interactive table, wrapped or not: a long float, such as 0.00015800000000000002 or 1.5207923835712901e-21, is shown to 6 significant digits, as 0.000158 or 1.52079E-21.
Scrolling is one of three ways i_responsive() fits a table to a narrow container; the others, stacking the rows as cards and dropping columns, are in Narrow containers.

    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with pinned columns")
    .i_cols_pin(columns="mfr")
    .i_cols_pin(columns="msrp", side="right")

Pinned columns have to be next to their side of the table, with only other pinned columns between them and it (as mfr is next to the stub, and msrp is the last column), so a column further in is moved there first, with cols_move_to_start() or cols_move_to_end(). Pinned columns can’t take up more than half of the table’s container; in a narrower one, only the stub stays pinned, until the container is wide enough again. The left is the stub’s side, so in a page written right to left, the columns pinned to the “left” are on the right, by the stub.


Narrow containers
A table wider than its container scrolls, as above, but i_responsive() has two other ways to fit it. With "stack", in a container narrower than stack_below= pixels (420, by default, as on a phone), each row becomes a card, titled by its stub, with each column’s label next to its value. Row groups become headings between the cards, and summary rows cards of their own. The column labels are shown above the cards as chips, which sort the table and open its filters as the labels do. Here, stack_below= is past this page’s width, so the cards are shown whatever its width; sort by HP with its chip, or filter by Make with the filter button on its chip.

(
    GTI(gtcars_pl, rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: stacked as cards")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_pagination(page_size=3)
    .i_responsive("stack", stack_below=2000)
)

A table is stacked by its CSS alone, so it’s stacked before its script runs (or without it). The column profiles aren’t shown on the cards, and a table in a container only as wide as what’s in it (a table’s cell, or an inline block) isn’t stacked, unless tab_options()’s container_width= gives it a width of its own. That width is the one stack_below= is compared with: a table with container_width="360px" is stacked in a wide page.
With "collapse", the table drops columns until it fits: first those without a priority from i_cols_priority() (from the last), then those with the highest numbers. A column with priority 1 is never dropped, nor is the stub. Each row gets a button by its first cell that shows the columns dropped from it, under it, as labels and values, and the columns come back as the container widens. Here’s the wide table of every column again, which keeps each car’s make and price, and its year and horsepower for as long as it can; it drops what this page has no room for, and more as the window narrows. Click the arrow by a car’s name to see what it dropped.

(
    gtcars_wide
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: dropping columns to fit")
    .i_cols_priority(columns=["mfr", "msrp"])
    .i_cols_priority(columns=["year", "hp"], priority=2)
    .i_responsive("collapse")
)

The dropped columns are still searched, filtered and exported. They’re dropped by the table’s script, so without it the table scrolls, as it does once only the columns that are never dropped are left. By default ("auto"), a table drops columns if any have a priority; otherwise it’s stacked below stack_below= if it shows no more than six columns (not counting the stub), and scrolls if it shows more.


Summary rows
A GTI table keeps the summary rows that summary_rows() and grand_summary_rows() add (see Summary Rows). The rows are sorted within their groups, and each group’s summary rows stay with it: those at its bottom are on the page where the group ends (and those at its top, on the page where it starts). The grand summary rows are on every page. Here, the most powerful cars of each country come first; page through to see each country’s averages, and the averages and highest values of all the cars under every page.

(
    GTI(gtcars_grouped, rowname_col="model", groupname_col="ctry_origin")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with summary rows")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .summary_rows(fns={"Average": pl.col("hp", "trq").mean()}, fmt=vals.fmt_integer)
    .grand_summary_rows(
        fns={"Average": pl.col("hp", "trq").mean(), "Highest": pl.col("hp", "trq").max()},
        fmt=vals.fmt_integer,
    )
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_view(sort="-hp")
)

Footnotes and source notes
A table’s footnotes and source notes are in its footer, as in a GT table, and the footnote marks stay with their cells as the rows are sorted, filtered and paged. Here, a footnote on the HP label says what it is, and another marks the cars of over 700 hp; sort by HP to bring them to the top.

    GTI(gtcars_pl)

    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .tab_footnote("Horsepower, at the engine's peak.", locations=loc.column_labels(columns="hp"))
    .tab_footnote("Over 700 hp.", locations=loc.body(columns="hp", rows=pl.col("hp") > 700))
    .tab_source_note("Source: the gtcars dataset.")

The marks are numbered as the table was first made, so a sorted table can have them out of order. The search doesn’t match them, and exports leave them out. A table of a lazy frame (a Polars LazyFrame, a DuckDB relation or an Ibis table), whose rows are collected as they’re shown, can have footnotes on its title, column labels and the rest, but not on its body or stub.


Row details
With i_row_details(), each row can have more to show under it, when the reader asks for it. A function makes a row’s details from its values (including those of columns the table hides): as text, with md() or html(), or as a GT table of their own. Here, each car has a few lines about its engine. Click the arrow by a car’s name to show them, or use Expand all in the table’s info panel to show every car’s.

from great_tables import md


def engine(row):
    economy = (
        "" if row["mpg_c"] is None else f" It gets {row['mpg_c']:.0f} mpg in the city, "
        f"and {row['mpg_h']:.0f} on the highway."
    )
    return md(
        f"The **{row['trim']}** ({row['bdy_style']}, {row['drivetrain'].upper()}) makes "
        f"{row['hp']:.0f} hp at {row['hp_rpm']:,.0f} rpm, and {row['trq']:.0f} lb-ft of torque."
        f"{economy}"
    )


(
    GTI(data.pl.gtcars, rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with row details")
    .cols_hide(
        columns=["trim", "bdy_style", "hp_rpm", "trq_rpm", "mpg_c", "mpg_h", "drivetrain", "trsmn"]
    )
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", ctry_origin="Country", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_row_details(engine)
)

The details are in the table’s HTML, made as it’s rendered, but aren’t searched, filtered or exported (and each GT table in them brings its own CSS, so many of them make a larger page). A column can hold them instead, with each row’s details: i_row_details() takes its name, and the column is then left out of the table.


Column profiles
With i_cols_profile(), columns get a small plot under their labels of how their values are spread: a histogram of numbers and dates, and bars for the most common values of the others, each with the share of rows that have a missing value. The plots follow the rows a search or filter keeps, so they show at a glance what’s left. Here, choose a few makes in the Make filter and watch the horsepower and prices narrow; point at a bar (or slide a finger along the plot) to see its values and its number of rows. A double click or double tap on a profile (or Enter on it) opens a larger view of it, with axes, the whole caption, and each bar’s rows.

(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with column profiles")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_profile(columns=["mfr", "year", "hp", "msrp"])
)

A profile’s bars span the whole column, not just the rows that are left, so that they stay put as the reader filters (only their heights change). They aren’t shown when the table is stacked as cards in a narrow container.


Choosing what readers can do with each column
Readers can sort, search and resize every column, by default, and hide or move none. With i_cols_controls(), each of these is set for the columns it’s given:

sortable=False takes away a column’s sort arrows (though i_view() can still sort by it)
searchable=False leaves the column’s cells out of the search (though its own filter still looks in them)
resizable=False keeps the column at its width, without a handle on its label
hideable=True puts a Columns button in the control bar, whose panel has a checkbox for each of the columns, to hide it or show it again
reorderable=True lists the columns in the same panel, in the order shown, where each can be dragged to another place, or moved with its arrow buttons (or Alt+↑ and Alt+↓)

Here, the search looks only at the cars’ names and makes, the make can’t be sorted by, and the numbers can be hidden and moved: open the Columns panel to show the city and highway mileage, or to put the price first.

gtcars_cols = data.pl.gtcars.select(
    ["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "trq", "mpg_c", "mpg_h", "msrp", "ctry_origin"]
)
numbers = ["year", "hp", "trq", "mpg_c", "mpg_h", "msrp"]

(
    GTI(gtcars_cols, rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: choosing the columns")
    .cols_label(
        mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", mpg_c="MPG City", mpg_h="MPG Highway",
        msrp="MSRP", ctry_origin="Country"
    )
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq", "mpg_c", "mpg_h"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_controls(columns="mfr", sortable=False)
    .i_cols_controls(columns=numbers, searchable=False, hideable=True, reorderable=True)
    .i_cols_controls(columns="ctry_origin", display=False)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="ctry_origin")
    .i_view(filter='ctry_origin in ("Italy", "Germany")', hidden=["mpg_c", "mpg_h"])
)

A hidden column is hidden in every row, the search doesn’t look in it, and exports leave it out, but a filter on it still keeps the rows it keeps. A column moves only among the movable columns next to it: it can’t leave its spanner, or pass a column readers can’t move. The table is first shown in the author’s order, and resetting the view goes back to it.
The country of origin here is in the data but not in the table, with display=False: it can’t be shown, but it can be filtered by (from its token in the bar, or the { } button), and the table can be sorted by it with i_view(), or by a view kept in the URL. The cars start filtered to those from Italy and Germany; remove the token to show them all. The search doesn’t look in such a column and exports leave it out, but the code copied for the view filters by it. This is also how a column that cols_hide() hid can be kept for querying.

A filtered table says what it’s filtered by with a token in its control bar (“Selected in Makes: Ferrari, Lamborghini”), which goes to the selection, and whose ✕ shows every row again (until the selection changes); its info panel says so too. The filter is on top of the table’s own search and filters, but isn’t part of its view, so it isn’t kept by i_view_state(). The tables link in the browser, with no server, so this works in a Quarto document or an HTML page, and in a notebook whose cells’ outputs share a page (in Jupyter, but not in Colab, which shows each cell’s output in a frame of its own).


How the rows look
i_display() sets how the table’s rows look:

highlight= (on by default) highlights the row under the pointer, or the row tapped on a touch screen
compact=True gives the rows half of their usual padding above and below, for more of them in view
wrap=False keeps each cell’s text on one line, cut short with an ellipsis if it doesn’t fit, so that every row is the same height
monospace=True puts the column labels and the cells in a monospaced font, for a table that’s a look at data more than a presentation of it (the title, the notes and the controls keep the table’s font)

a CSV or TSV file has the column labels as its first row (each after its spanners’ labels, as in “Revenue – gross”), and with row groups, the group’s label as a column before the others; a cell a spreadsheet would read as a formula starts with a ', so that it’s read as text
a JSON file has an object for each row, with each cell’s text under its column’s name in the data (and the row’s group label first, under "group")
a copy has the rows both as a table, with the cells’ styles, for pasting into a document or a spreadsheet, and as text, with tabs between the cells
the code filters and sorts the data (as df) as the reader’s view does, for Polars, Pandas or Narwhals (the data’s library, at first); it works on the data’s values, so it leaves out the search

The formats’ buttons are in the order i_export() is given them. With i_selection(), readers can export the rows they’ve selected instead.


Using the table from Python and in apps
Python can read what readers do with a GTI table and change it: in a notebook, with the table as a widget, in a marimo notebook, and in Shiny, Streamlit, Panel and Solara apps; and a page an app makes itself, with Flask, Django or FastHTML, can show it. See GTI in Python and Apps, where a marimo notebook and a Streamlit and a Panel app with a GTI table can be run in the browser, to see a selection reach Python and Python sort the table.

title: Header, Footer, and Stub
text:
Three structural components frame the data in your table: the Table Header introduces it with a title and optional subtitle, the Table Footer anchors it with source notes or other supplementary information, and the Stub provides a left-hand column of row identifiers. All three are added using the tab_*() family of methods.


A well-structured frame transforms a bare data grid into something self-explanatory. Without these components, your reader has to look outside the table for context: what is this data? Where did it come from? What do the rows represent? Adding a header, footer, and stub answers those questions inside the table itself, so it can stand on its own in a report, slide deck, or web page.

Adding a Table Header
A Table Header is easy to add with the tab_header() method. Let’s see how a basic table looks with a title and a subtitle:

import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT, data, md

# Get the ten most populous countries in 2022
countries_mini = (
    data.pl.countrypops.filter(pl.col("year") == 2022)
    .sort("population", descending=True)
    .head(10)
    .select("country_name", "population")
)

# Make a display table with the `countries_mini` table and
# put a heading just above the column labels
(
    GT(countries_mini)
    .tab_header(
        title="The World's Most Populous Countries",
        subtitle="The top ten in 2022 are presented"
    )
)






  
    The World's Most Populous Countries
  
  
    The top ten in 2022 are presented
  

  country_name
  population



  
    India
    1417173173
  
  
    China
    1412175000
  
  
    United States
    333287557
  
  
    Indonesia
    275501339
  
  
    Pakistan
    235824862
  
  
    Nigeria
    218541212
  
  
    Brazil
    215313498
  
  
    Bangladesh
    171186372
  
  
    Russian Federation
    143555736
  
  
    Mexico
    127504125
  







As a rule of thumb, any table that will be seen outside your own notebook benefits from a title. It also immediately orients the reader as to what the table’s all about.
The Header provides an opportunity to describe the data that’s presented. Using subtitle= allows us to insert a subtitle, which is an optional part of the Header. We may also style the title= and subtitle= using Markdown! We do this by wrapping the values passed to title= or subtitle= with the md() helper function (we may also use html() in a similar fashion). Here is an example with the table data truncated for brevity:

# Make a display table with the `countries_mini` table and
# put a heading just above the column labels
gt_tbl = (
    GT(countries_mini.head(2))
    .tab_header(
        title=md("The *World's* Most Populous Countries 🌐"),
        subtitle=md("The top **ten** in 2022 are presented")
    )
)

gt_tbl






  
    The World's Most Populous Countries 🌐
  
  
    The top ten in 2022 are presented
  

  country_name
  population



  
    India
    1417173173
  
  
    China
    1412175000
  







With a title and subtitle in place, the reader immediately knows what the table is about before looking at any data.


Adding Source Notes
A source note can be added to the table’s Footer through use of the tab_source_note() method. It works in the same way as tab_header() (it also allows for Markdown inputs) except it can be called multiple times. Each invocation results in the addition of a source note.

# Display the `countries_mini` data with a heading and two source notes
(
    gt_tbl
    .tab_source_note(
        source_note="Total population counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship."
    )
    .tab_source_note(
        source_note=md("Source: [The World Bank](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL).")
    )
)






  
    The World's Most Populous Countries 🌐
  
  
    The top ten in 2022 are presented
  

  country_name
  population



  
    India
    1417173173
  
  
    China
    1412175000
  

Total population counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship.Source: The World Bank.





Source notes are pretty valuable because they provide provenance and credibility. Academic and business audiences might expect to know where data comes from. Including that information directly in the table saves readers from hunting through surrounding text. Source notes are also a good place for methodological caveats or disclaimers that apply to the entire table.
With just a few method calls, we have added essential context to the table. The title and subtitle tell the reader what data is being presented, and the source notes provide attribution. Together, these components frame the table body and help your audience understand the data at a glance.


The Stub: Row Labels
The Stub is good to have whenever the first column of your data serves as an identifier rather than a measured value. Moving identifiers into the stub visually separates “what this row is about” from “what was measured”, making the table easier to scan. If your rows represent people, places, time periods, or categories, those labels would go nicely in the stub.
The Stub is the area to the left of the table body that typically contains row labels and may also contain row group labels. Those subparts can be grouped in a sequence of row groups. The Stub Head provides a location for a label that describes the Stub (and could also be used to describe the column labels). The Stub is optional since there are cases where it wouldn’t be useful (the display tables presented earlier looked just fine without one).
An easy way to generate a Stub part is by naming a stub column with the rowname_col= argument of the tab_stub() method. This will signal to Great Tables that the named column should be used as the stub, using the contents of that column to make row labels. Let’s add a stub to our countries_mini table:

GT(countries_mini).tab_stub(rowname_col="country_name")







  
  population



  
    India
    1417173173
  
  
    China
    1412175000
  
  
    United States
    333287557
  
  
    Indonesia
    275501339
  
  
    Pakistan

    Nigeria
    218541212

    215313498
  
  
    Bangladesh
    171186372
  
  
    Russian Federation
    143555736
  
  
    Mexico
    127504125
  







Notice that the country names are now placed to the left? That’s the Stub. Notably, there is a prominent border to the right of it but there’s no label above the Stub. We can change this and apply what’s known as a stubhead label through use of the tab_stubhead() method:

(
    GT(countries_mini)
    .tab_stub(rowname_col="country_name")
    .tab_stubhead(label="country")
)

  population

A very important thing to note here is that the table now has one column. Before, when there was no Stub, two columns were present (with the Column Labels of "country_name" and "population") but now column number 1 (the only column remaining) is population.


Row Groups
Grouping is most useful when your data has a natural categorical structure and you want readers to compare within and across categories. Rather than forcing the reader to mentally sort the rows, row groups do that work up front.
Let’s incorporate row groups into the display table. This divides rows into groups, creating row groups, and results in a display of row group labels right above each group. This can be easily done with a table containing row labels and the key is to use the groupname_col= argument of tab_stub(). Here we will create four row groups (with row group labels "Asia", "Americas", "Africa", and "Europe") to have a grouping of rows.

regions = {
    "India": "Asia", "China": "Asia", "Indonesia": "Asia", "Pakistan": "Asia",
    "Bangladesh": "Asia", "United States": "Americas", "Brazil": "Americas",
    "Mexico": "Americas", "Nigeria": "Africa", "Russian Federation": "Europe",
}

country_groups = countries_mini.with_columns(
    region=pl.col("country_name").replace_strict(regions)
)

(
    GT(country_groups)
    .tab_stub(rowname_col="country_name", groupname_col="region")
    .tab_stubhead(label="country")
)







  country
  population



  
    Asia
  
  
    India

title: Making Tables Interactive
text:
Great Tables can make a table that readers work with in the browser: sorting it by its columns, searching and filtering its rows, and paging through them. The table is the one you made, with all its formatting, styles and structure; a small script that comes with its HTML adds the controls. Nothing else is needed to view it (no server, internet connection, or other library), and the table can be read before the script runs, or if it never does. It’s interactive wherever its HTML is shown: in Jupyter notebooks, Quarto documents, and HTML files written with write_raw_html().
Interactive tables are ideal for exploratory contexts where the reader needs to find specific values in a larger dataset (e.g., dashboards, internal tools, or notebook-based analysis). Sorting and filtering let readers answer their own questions about the data without you having to anticipate every view. For static outputs like PDF reports, printed documents, or email, stick with static tables since the interactivity features won’t be functional in those formats.

title: Introduction
text:
The Great Tables package is all about making it simple to produce nice-looking display tables. Display tables? Well yes, we are trying to distinguish between data tables (i.e., DataFrames) and those tables you’d find in a web page, a journal article, or in a magazine. Such tables can likewise be called presentation tables, summary tables, or just tables really. Here are some examples, ripped straight from the web:



A collage of display tables taken from web pages, articles, and magazines.




Display tables exist because raw DataFrames are working artifacts, not communication tools. When you share findings with colleagues, stakeholders, or readers, the formatting of your table directly affects how well your message lands. Good structure and styling reduce cognitive load, draw attention to what matters, and help your audience reach the right conclusions faster. A well-built table is an act of respect for your reader’s time.
We can think of display tables as output only, where we’d not want to use them as input ever again. Other features include annotations, table element styling, and text transformations that serve to communicate the subject matter more clearly.

Let’s Install
The installation really couldn’t be much easier. Use this:
pip install great_tables
Once installed, you are ready to build your first table.


A Basic Table using Great Tables
Let’s use a subset of the countrypops dataset available within great_tables.data, keeping the ten most populous countries in 2022:

import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT, data

countries_mini = (
    data.pl.countrypops.filter(pl.col("year") == 2022)
    .sort("population", descending=True)
    .head(10)
    .select("country_name", "population")
)

The countries_mini data is a simple Polars DataFrame with 2 columns and that’ll serve as a great start. Speaking of which, the main entry point into the Great Tables API is the GT class. Let’s use that to make a presentable table:

# Create a display table showing the ten most populous countries
gt_tbl = GT(countries_mini)

# Show the output table
gt_tbl

  population

That doesn’t look too bad! Sure, it’s basic but we really didn’t ask for much. We did receive a proper table with column labels and the data. Even this minimal output is an improvement over a raw DataFrame: you get proper HTML rendering, consistent spacing, and a clean visual structure that works in notebooks, reports, and web pages alike. But the real power of Great Tables comes from layering on the structural components described next. Oftentimes, you’ll want a bit more: a Table Header, a Stub, and sometimes source notes in the Table Footer component.






Note



Typically we use Great Tables in a notebook environment or within a Quarto document. Tables won’t print to the console, but using the show() method on a table object while in the console will open the HTML table in your default browser.




Polars, Pandas, and PyArrow support
GT accepts Polars and Pandas DataFrames, as well as PyArrow tables, and none of these libraries is a hard requirement: install whichever one you already use. Supporting several backends matters because teams often have mixed workflows, and you shouldn’t have to rewrite your table code just because a project uses a different DataFrame library. This User Guide mostly uses Polars, but the table-building code is the same whichever DataFrame you start from.
A Polars DataFrame can also be turned into a table through its DataFrame.style property:

GT(countries_mini)
